replies.author: @Bawang73
replies.text:
@Feelingoodagain Okay. Let me elaborate. Most people frame failure to repay as a moral failure. It isn’t. It is a business decision. These banks don’t operate on morality… at all. Most Americans haven’t really done the math on DAILY compounding interest, and that is, in part, the failure of the individual. However, our society has NORMALIZED debt, meaning, we are programmed to take on debt. Credit card companies solicit through the mail, and through email. Visa and Mastercard’s profit margin is 45 to 55 percent. The issuing banks make about 25 percent. With merchant’s fees, they can’t lose. Then, you need to look at what the average interest rate is. Legally, it isn’t usury, thanks to our corrupt politicians and the Monetary Control Act of 1980, but, in the classical sense, it absolutely is. If you want to make the moral argument, you have to make it for both sides. Is it moral to lend to someone at interest rates that a reasonable person would call usury? No, of course not. But, they do it. To them, it is just business. 

So, insofar as the illegal aliens are concerned. Let’s look at the morality. Is it moral to give loans to people you know who are extremely likely to default, and then pass the financial burden on to other consumers when they do default? No, of course not, but that is exactly what happens. Most people agree that the banks were doing predatory lending prior to the 2008 financial crisis, but you can’t see that they are doing something equally as insidious with their lending practices? And, don’t get me started on how abusive variable APRs are. 

You tell people living in a civilization where financial literacy isn’t taught in school, where debt is normalized, where banks target people through solicitations, where the terms are confusing to the average person, and where most people can’t afford to set aside a small emergency fund, because our politicians are insane when it comes to debt… you’re telling those people to not use a credit card if they hit a crisis like a medical bill, or a car breaking down, or a heater that goes out during the winter, or an air conditioner that stops working during the hottest summer months. You are telling people who live in a debt economy not to use debt. That’s rich. That is like telling them not to breathe. The system is rigged so that it is nearly impossible to take on some kind of debt.

You tell me where, in this economy, people are supposed to find the funds to buy a car with cash, a house with cash, or the money to pay a ten thousand dollar medical copay with cash. I mean, we live in a service based economy, so tell me where they are supposed to get that kind of money fresh out of school. Also, how are they supposed to avoid student loans, when the price of college is insane? That’s another system that is predatory, because it is supported by government loan programs, but I’m sure you’d shill for that system too. It would be somehow the student’s fault for daring to want an education, for daring to want to change their circumstances long term. 

You are arguing for a system that is predatory, uncaring, immoral, and usurious. The original poster wants people to go to prison for defaulting. Okay, fine. What about the bankers? Oh, nothing for them, of course. They are somehow the innocent victims in all of this. LOL

You don’t see the logic, because you don’t understand the system as well as you think you do. I see default as a strategic exit. To the banks, it is business, and, historically, banks have been bailed out with public funds when they wind up in a bind. Funny how that works. Again, they can’t lose. They have the system rigged that way. It is all rigged against you, and you want to shill for it. 

Any time I see someone get one in against the system, I say good for them. 

Debtor’s prison, indeed. LOL
